title: MMRM (Mixed-Effect Model for Repeated Measures)
dependent: Dependent variable (continuous longitudinal outcome, e.g. change from baseline)
treatment: Treatment / group variable (must be a factor)
visit: Visit / time variable (categorical time, must be a factor)
subject: Subject identifier (repeated measures are correlated within this unit)
cov: Covariance structure (for correlated residuals within subject)
groupCov: Estimate a separate covariance matrix for each level of the treatment variable
method: Method for degrees of freedom / small-sample adjustment
label2: Options for least square means and treatment contrasts
anovachk: Type III ANOVA (Wald tests of fixed effects)
lsmeanschk: Least square (estimated marginal) means and treatment contrasts by visit
diagplotchk: Diagnostic plots (residuals vs fitted, normal Q-Q)

help.title: MMRM (Mixed-Effect Model for Repeated Measures)
help.body:
What is an MMRM?
A Mixed-Effect Model for Repeated Measures (MMRM) analyzes a continuous outcome that is measured on the same subjects at several fixed time points, and asks how that outcome differs between groups over time. Instead of collapsing each subject to a single number, it uses every visit and accounts for the fact that repeated measurements on one person are correlated. It models the average response through fixed effects (usually treatment, visit, and their interaction, plus baseline covariates) and captures the within-subject correlation directly through a residual covariance structure across visits, rather than through per-subject random effects. A key practical advantage is that, under a Missing at Random assumption, it uses all the data a subject did provide without discarding them or filling in the missing visits, which is why regulatory agencies widely accept it.

A clinical trial example
Suppose a trial measures a symptom score at Baseline, Week 4, Week 8, and Week 12 for patients on an active drug versus placebo, and the endpoint is the change from baseline at Week 12. Patients inevitably drop out, so many have some visits missing. An MMRM with treatment, visit, and the treatment-by-visit interaction estimates the treatment difference at each visit while borrowing strength across the correlated visits and across patients, giving a valid Week 12 treatment effect that uses the partial data from patients who left early. The result is usually summarised as the least-square-mean difference between arms at the final visit. This is the standard primary-analysis approach for longitudinal continuous endpoints in psychiatry, neurology, and many other therapeutic areas.

Description
Builds a Mixed-Effect Model for Repeated Measures (MMRM), the standard method for analyzing longitudinal continuous outcomes (e.g. change from baseline in a symptom score) measured at several discrete visits in a clinical trial. Internally calls the mmrm() function from the mmrm package and stores the result in an object with the name you specify.

An MMRM models the mean through fixed effects (typically treatment, visit, and the treatment-by-visit interaction, plus baseline covariates) and models the within-subject correlation directly through a residual covariance structure rather than through subject-level random effects. Under a Missing at Random (MAR) assumption it uses all observed data and produces valid treatment-effect estimates without imputing missing visits, which is why it is widely accepted by regulatory agencies.

NOTE
1. The data must be in the long format, one row per subject per visit. See Datasets > ReShape > Longer.
2. The visit variable and the treatment variable must be factors. See Data > Factor Levels to convert and to reorder levels (the first level of the treatment variable is normally the control/reference arm).
3. Rows with a missing outcome are used by the model implicitly under MAR; they are not imputed and should not be deleted.
4. Unlike repeated measures ANOVA, an MMRM with an unstructured covariance does not assume sphericity or homogeneity of variances, so tests such as Box's M, Levene's and Brown-Forsythe are not applicable here.

Usage
library(mmrm)
MMRMModel1 <- mmrm(
  formula = CHG ~ ARM + AVISIT + BASE + ARM:AVISIT + us(AVISIT | USUBJID),
  data = Dataset1,
  method = "Satterthwaite",
  vcov = "Asymptotic",
  reml = TRUE)
#Summarizing the model
summary(MMRMModel1)
#Type III tests of fixed effects
car::Anova(MMRMModel1, type = "III")
#Least square means and treatment contrasts by visit
emmeans::emmeans(MMRMModel1, ~ ARM | AVISIT)
Arguments
  • Dependent variable: The continuous outcome measured repeatedly over time. In clinical trials this is usually the change from baseline of the endpoint of interest.
  • Treatment / group variable: The fixed effect whose effect on the outcome you want to estimate (e.g. treatment arm). It must be a factor.
  • Visit / time variable: The categorical time variable (e.g. Baseline, Week 4, Week 8, Week 12). It must be a factor. It appears both as a fixed effect and inside the covariance term.
  • Subject identifier: The variable that identifies each patient. Repeated measurements taken on the same subject are allowed to be correlated; this variable is the grouping unit of the covariance structure. Each subject/visit combination must appear at most once.
  • Baseline covariate(s): Optional additional fixed effects to adjust for, such as the baseline value of the endpoint or stratification factors.
Covariance structures
The mmrm package supplies the within-subject covariance through a function of the form <structure>(visit | subject). Available choices in this dialog:
  • Unstructured (us): every variance and covariance estimated freely. The default and gold standard.
  • Compound symmetry (cs) / heterogeneous compound symmetry (csh).
  • Autoregressive order 1 (ar1) / heterogeneous AR(1) (ar1h).
  • Toeplitz (toep) / heterogeneous Toeplitz (toeph).
  • Ante-dependence, heterogeneous (adh).
If you check the option to estimate a separate covariance matrix per treatment group, the covariance term becomes <structure>(visit | treatment / subject). This is useful when the arms are expected to have different variability over time, but it estimates many more parameters.

Method
Controls the denominator degrees of freedom and small-sample adjustment for the Wald tests: Satterthwaite (default), Kenward-Roger, Residual, or Between-Within.

Coefficient covariance
Asymptotic (default) uses the model-based standard errors. The Empirical options request robust "sandwich" standard errors, which are less sensitive to a misspecified covariance structure. Kenward-Roger coefficient covariance is only available when the method is Kenward-Roger.

Trying it out with the fev_data dataset
The mmrm package ships a sample dataset, fev_data, which is ideal for trying this dialog. Load it into BlueSky (or run data(fev_data, package = "mmrm") in the R editor and use it as your dataset). It is already in the long format, one row per subject per visit, and contains a continuous outcome FEV1 with genuinely missing values from dropout.

Before running, use Data > Factor Levels to confirm that ARMCD (treatment) and AVISIT (visit) are factors, and that the first level of ARMCD is the control arm you want as the reference.

Select the variables into the input fields as follows:
  • Dependent variable: FEV1 (the repeated continuous outcome; it has missing values, which is expected).
  • Treatment / group variable: ARMCD (levels PBO and TRT; PBO is the reference).
  • Visit / time variable: AVISIT (VIS1 through VIS4).
  • Subject identifier: USUBJID.
  • Baseline covariate(s): FEV1_BL and RACE (optionally SEX).
Leave WEIGHT, VISITN and VISITN2 in the source list.

Options to select: keep Include treatment-by-visit interaction checked (this is the core of an MMRM); leave Estimate a separate covariance matrix for each level of the treatment variable unchecked; set the covariance structure to Unstructured (us), the method to Satterthwaite, the coefficient covariance to Asymptotic, and the estimator to REML. In the options tab, useful choices are Type III ANOVA and Least square means and treatment contrasts by visit; you can also tick Display estimated residual covariance matrix and Diagnostic plots to see the full output.

With these settings the model that is fitted is FEV1 ~ ARMCD + AVISIT + FEV1_BL + RACE + ARMCD:AVISIT + us(AVISIT | USUBJID). You should see the fixed-effect coefficients, the model fit statistics (note that three subjects whose outcome is missing at every visit are dropped, so the subjects used will be fewer than the total in the data), the Type III tests, and the least-square means with treatment contrasts at each visit. To see robust standard errors, rerun with the coefficient covariance set to Empirical: the estimates stay the same while the standard errors change.
